analogy.p: Think of stem cells as a stack of **blank, un-badged staff uniforms** in a hospital store room. Until a uniform is given a badge and a name (a nurse, a porter, a surgeon) it could become any of them: that is differentiation. The store room can also make more blank uniforms (division by mitosis). A meristem is like a factory that keeps making blank uniforms for life, while a bone marrow is a store that only supplies certain kinds. The analogy breaks down because a uniform is an object that is simply labelled, whereas a cell actually changes its structure and switches on different genes when it differentiates, and in animals this change is usually permanent.
analogy.t: Stem cells as blank trainee uniforms

bullets: **Undifferentiated** = not specialised; the cell has not yet developed the features (shape, sub-cellular structures) needed for one particular job.
**Capable of dividing** by **mitosis** to make many more cells; the daughter cells are genetically identical to the parent.
**Capable of differentiating**: some of the new cells can then become specialised cells such as nerve cells or red blood cells.
The two key properties (divide + differentiate) are what make stem cells so useful for **growth, repair and replacement** of tissue.
Mark scheme wording to use: 'an **undifferentiated** cell that can **divide** and **differentiate** into other types of cell'.
Do not confuse **stem cell** (can become other cell types) with a **specialised cell** (adapted for one job and usually cannot change).
core.h: What a stem cell is (the definition to learn word for word)
core.p: A **stem cell** is an **undifferentiated cell of an organism which is capable of giving rise to many more cells of the same type, and from which certain other cells can arise from differentiation**. 'Undifferentiated' means the cell has not yet become specialised for one job, so it has no fixed shape or special sub-cellular structures. Because it is unspecialised, it can still follow different pathways and turn into different kinds of cell. Every one of the specialised cells in your body (nerve, muscle, blood, skin) started as a stem cell in an early embryo.

bullets: Differentiation = the process by which a cell becomes **specialised** to carry out a particular function.
Specialisation depends on **which genes are switched on**; all body cells contain the same DNA, but different genes are expressed in different cell types.
In most **animals** the ability to differentiate is **lost at an early stage**; once specialised, cells generally only divide to produce more of the same cell type.
In **mature plants** many types of cell **retain the ability to differentiate** throughout life (this is why plant stem cells in meristems are so useful).
Specialised cells have **different numbers of sub-cellular structures** (e.g. many mitochondria in muscle cells for energy release; many ribosomes in cells making protein).
Stem cells are the cells that **avoid** early differentiation, so they act like a reserve supply of new specialised cells.
core.p: As most animal embryos develop, cells **differentiate**: they change to become specialised for a particular function. They do this by developing the **sub-cellular structures** they need, for example a sperm cell develops a tail (flagellum) and many mitochondria, and a red blood cell loses its nucleus to make room for haemoglobin. In most animals, differentiation happens early and the **ability to differentiate is then lost** in almost all cells, so a muscle cell cannot turn into a nerve cell. Many adult animal cells can only divide to replace themselves (repair and replacement), which is why stem cells are so valuable.

bullets: Source: **early human embryos** (often unused embryos left over from IVF fertility treatment).
Potential: can differentiate into **most (almost all) types of human cell**, which is why they are the most powerful type for research and treatment.
They can be **cloned** (grown in large numbers) in the lab and made to **differentiate** into the specialised cells needed to treat a patient.
Potential uses: replacing damaged **nerve cells** (e.g. paralysis caused by spinal injury), **insulin-producing cells** (diabetes), and other damaged or lost tissues.
Main objection: taking the stem cells **destroys the embryo**, which some people believe is a potential human life.
Risk: stem cells grown in the lab may be contaminated with a **virus**, which could be passed to the patient.
core.p: **Embryonic stem cells** are taken from **early human embryos** (a ball of cells just a few days old). At this stage every cell is undifferentiated, so these cells can **differentiate into most types of human cell**. Scientists can grow them in the lab and use chemical signals to push them to become a chosen cell type. They are the most flexible stem cells but also the most controversial because obtaining them destroys the embryo.

bullets: Source: **bone marrow** of adults (taken from a donor or the patient).
Potential: can form **many types of cell, including blood cells**, but not as many types as embryonic stem cells.
Use: **bone marrow transplants** to treat blood diseases, e.g. **sickle cell anaemia**.
Adult stem cells can be taken from a person and used for that same person, avoiding most rejection problems; donor cells may be **rejected** if not a close match.
Fewer ethical objections than embryonic stem cells because **no embryo is destroyed**.
Limitation: restricted range of cell types they can become, and they may be harder to grow in large numbers.
core.p: **Adult stem cells** are found in some adult tissues. The example you must know is the **bone marrow**, where stem cells can form **many types of cell including blood cells** (red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets). Adult stem cells are less flexible than embryonic stem cells because they can only form a limited range of cells, but collecting them does not destroy an embryo.

bullets: Location: **meristems** at the **tips of shoots and roots**.
They can differentiate into **any type of plant cell** (xylem, phloem, palisade, root hair etc.).
They can do this **throughout the life of the plant**, so plants grow continually.
Uses: to produce **clones** of the plant quickly and economically (see tissue culture below).
Remember: the plant cells that make up a leaf or root hair are specialised, but meristem cells remain **undifferentiated**.
Meristem cells also divide by **mitosis**, so the clones are genetically identical.
core.p: In plants, stem cells are found in **meristem tissue**, located at the **tips of roots and shoots** (where growth in length happens). Meristem cells can **differentiate into any type of plant cell, and they do so throughout the whole life of the plant**. This is a big difference from animals, where the ability is mostly lost early. The ability explains why plants can keep growing and why a cutting can grow into a whole new plant.

bullets: **Embryonic**: from early embryos; most human cell types; ethical objections because the embryo is destroyed.
**Adult (bone marrow)**: from adults; many cell types including blood cells; used for bone marrow transplants.
**Meristem (plant)**: tips of roots and shoots; any plant cell type; active throughout life; used for cloning plants.
Range of potential: embryonic > adult (bone marrow); meristem is 'any plant cell' for plants.
All are **undifferentiated** and can divide by **mitosis**, producing genetically identical daughter cells.
Only **embryonic** and **adult** stem cells are used to treat human disease; meristems are used in **agriculture and conservation**.
core.p: It helps to compare the sources directly because exam questions often ask 'which type of stem cell…?'. **Embryonic** stem cells have the widest potential (most human cell types) but raise the biggest ethical issues. **Adult** stem cells in bone marrow have a narrower range (many cell types including blood cells) with fewer ethical issues. **Plant meristems** can become any plant cell and are used to clone plants. All three are undifferentiated cells that divide by mitosis.

bullets: Bone marrow stem cells of a healthy donor are transferred to the patient.
The donor stem cells **divide and differentiate** into healthy red blood cells.
This can **cure** diseases such as sickle cell anaemia by providing a lasting supply of normal cells.
Risk: a **virus** may be transferred from the donor cells to the patient and make them ill.
Risk: if the donor is not a close match, the patient's immune system may **reject** the transplanted cells.
The treatment is already used in hospitals, unlike many embryonic stem cell treatments, which are still being researched.
core.h: Treating human disease: bone marrow transplants
core.p: **Sickle cell anaemia** is an inherited disorder where red blood cells have an abnormal shape and cannot carry oxygen properly. Stem cells from the bone marrow of a healthy **donor** can be transplanted into the patient. These stem cells divide and differentiate to produce **normal red blood cells**, which can treat or cure the disease. This is an example of stem cells being used to **replace faulty cells**.

bullets: Embryo produced with the **same genes as the patient** (genetically identical).
**Embryonic stem cells** are taken from the embryo and made to **differentiate** into the required cells.
Advantage: the cells are **not rejected** because the immune system does not see them as foreign, so there is no need for **immunosuppressant** drugs.
Possible uses: **insulin-producing cells** for diabetes; **nerve cells** for paralysis.
Disadvantages: the **embryo is destroyed**, treatments are still being developed, and the risk of **viral contamination** remains.
Therapeutic cloning is different from **reproductive cloning**, which aims to create a whole new individual; therapeutic cloning is only to create cells for treatment.
core.p: **Therapeutic cloning** involves producing an **embryo with the same genes as the patient**. Stem cells from this embryo are then used to make the cells the patient needs. Because the cells have the same genes as the patient, they are **not rejected by the patient's body** (the immune system recognises them as 'self'), so they can be used for medical treatment. The embryo is destroyed in the process, which is the main ethical problem.

bullets: Diabetes: stem cells could be turned into **insulin-producing cells** to replace the lost cells.
Paralysis: stem cells could be turned into **nerve cells** to repair damaged nerve tissue.
Other possibilities: damaged heart tissue, eye and joint problems, and growing organs for transplant.
Benefits: could reduce the need for **donor organs**, reduce long waiting lists, and treat conditions currently incurable.
Uncertainty: stem cells may **divide out of control** and form tumours; research is still ongoing.
Always use tentative language in exam answers: 'could', 'may help', 'potential'.
core.p: Scientists think stem cells could treat conditions where specialised cells have been lost or damaged. AQA names **diabetes** (type 1: the pancreas does not make enough insulin, so insulin-producing cells could be made from stem cells) and **paralysis** (nerve cells damaged in spinal injury could be replaced). These are possibilities, not guaranteed cures, so use cautious words like 'could' and 'may'.

bullets: Against: embryo has the **potential to become a person**; some religions believe life begins at conception.
Against: risk of **viral transfer**, uncertain long-term safety, cost of treatments, and fear of 'slippery slope' towards human cloning.
For: could **cure or treat serious diseases** and improve quality of life for many people.
For: embryos used are mostly **surplus from IVF** and would otherwise be thrown away.
For: **adult stem cells** and cloned plant cells avoid the main objection (no embryo destroyed).
Decisions are made by society and governed by **laws and regulations**; science can tell us what is possible but not whether it is right.
In evaluate questions, give at least one point for and against and finish with a **justified conclusion**.
core.p: Many people object to embryonic stem cell research on **ethical or religious grounds**. The main argument is that an embryo is a **potential human life**, so destroying it is wrong. Supporters argue that the embryos used are usually **unwanted embryos from fertility clinics** that would be destroyed anyway, and that the potential to cure serious diseases and relieve suffering outweighs the loss. You need to be able to give both sides in a balanced way.

bullets: Rare species: meristem cloning can make many copies of a plant when few individuals exist, to **prevent extinction**.
Crop plants: farmers can grow **large numbers of identical plants** with desirable features, e.g. **disease resistance**, in bulk.
The clones are **genetically identical** to the parent, so the useful feature is guaranteed.
It is **quick and economical** compared with waiting for seeds to grow.
Disadvantage: little **genetic variation**, so one disease could wipe out all the clones.
Sterile conditions are needed, otherwise **microbes** will grow in the nutrient-rich medium and kill the tissue.
core.p: **Meristem tissue** can be used to **produce clones of a plant quickly and economically**. A small piece of meristem is taken from the parent plant and grown in a sterile culture medium (such as agar with nutrients and hormones). The cells divide by mitosis to make many identical plantlets. This is called **tissue culture**. AQA gives two uses: saving **rare species from extinction** and growing **crop plants with special features** (such as disease resistance) in large numbers.

bullets: **Virus transfer**: a virus in the donor cells could infect the patient and make them ill.
**Rejection**: non-matching cells are attacked by the immune system; solved by therapeutic cloning (same genes).
**Embryo destruction**: ethical objection; avoided by adult stem cells.
**Uncontrolled division**: stem cells could cause tumours, so extensive testing is needed.
**Cost and availability**: treatments are expensive and still under development.
**Reduced diversity (plants)**: cloned crops are vulnerable to a single disease.
core.h: Risks and limitations: summary table in words
core.p: Examiners like you to link a benefit with a matching drawback. The main **risks** of stem cell treatments are **viral infection** (a virus may be passed from donor cells to the patient), **rejection** if cells are not a match, and the possibility that the cells **divide uncontrollably**. The main **social** issues are the destruction of embryos and religious beliefs. Plant stem cells carry fewer concerns but reduce genetic diversity.

bullets: Mitosis: stem cells divide by mitosis to make genetically identical copies.
Cloning: plant tissue culture uses meristems to produce clones.
Diabetes: link to the endocrine system and insulin from the pancreas.
Genetics: therapeutic cloning produces cells with the **same genes** as the patient.
Evaluate = weigh up **advantages and disadvantages** and reach a judgement.
Plan 6-mark answers: define, uses, benefits, risks, ethics, conclusion.
core.h: Links to other topics and how to answer evaluation questions
core.p: Stem cells link to **mitosis and the cell cycle** (stem cells divide by mitosis), to **asexual reproduction and cloning** (plant tissue culture), to **genetics** (identical genes mean no rejection) and to **ethics in science**. For a 6-mark question, structure your answer as: what stem cells are, benefits, risks/ethical issues, then a conclusion. Use specific named examples (sickle cell anaemia, diabetes, paralysis, rare species).

exam: **State/Name (1 mark)**: give one precise word or phrase, e.g. 'meristem', 'bone marrow'.
**Define a stem cell (1-2 marks)**: 'an **undifferentiated** cell that can **divide** to make more cells and **differentiate** into specialised cells'.
**Describe a use (2 marks)**: name the stem cell source, the cell it becomes, and the disease: 'bone marrow stem cells differentiate into red blood cells to treat sickle cell anaemia'.
**Explain why therapeutic cloning avoids rejection (2-3 marks)**: embryo has the **same genes** as the patient, so cells are not seen as foreign by the **immune system**.
**Give a risk (1 mark)**: 'a **virus** may be transferred from the donor cells to the patient'.

**Explain meristem cloning (3-4 marks)**: take meristem cells, grow in sterile medium, cells divide by mitosis, produce genetically identical plants; use for **rare species** or **disease-resistant crops**.
**Evaluate (6 marks)**: give benefits and risks/ethical issues and a final judgement; use named examples; use 'could' for future uses.
**Command words**: Describe = say what; Explain = give reasons (use 'because'); Evaluate = weigh both sides and conclude; Give = short answer.
Do not say stem cells are 'identical' to each other; say they are **undifferentiated**.
Mention both **ethical** and **scientific** points in discussion answers; avoid personal opinion without reasons.

mistakes.r: An **undifferentiated cell** that can **divide** and **differentiate** into other cell types; embryonic can form most human cell types, adult only a range.
mistakes.w: Stem cells are 'special cells that can turn into anything'.

mistakes.r: Stem cells are **unspecialised/undifferentiated**; specialised cells have already differentiated.
Bone marrow stem cells can form **many types of cell including blood cells**, but not as many as embryonic stem cells.
mistakes.w: Adult stem cells can become any cell in the body.

mistakes.r: **Meristem tissue** is found at the **tips of roots and shoots** and contains stem cells that can become any plant cell.
mistakes.w: Meristem is the 'stem' of a plant.

mistakes.r: It produces an **embryo with the patient's genes** only to obtain stem cells for **treatment**; the cells are **not rejected**.
mistakes.w: Therapeutic cloning makes a whole new person.

mistakes.r: They **could/may** be used to treat these in future; use tentative wording.
mistakes.w: Stem cells cure diabetes and paralysis now.

mistakes.r: Risk is **virus transfer** from donor cells; rejection is avoided by therapeutic cloning (same genes).
mistakes.w: The risk is that stem cells 'might be rejected' (for all types).

mistakes.r: Embryos are **destroyed**; some believe an embryo is a **potential human life** (ethical/religious grounds).
mistakes.w: Ethical objection is that stem cells 'hurt' people.

summary: AQA wants you to know that a **stem cell** is an **undifferentiated** cell that can divide to make more cells of the same type and can **differentiate** into specialised cells. You must know the three sources (**embryonic**, **adult bone marrow**, **plant meristems**), how they are used in medicine (including **therapeutic cloning**) and in plant cloning, and be able to discuss the risks and the ethical or religious objections. It matters because 'evaluate the use of stem cells' is a classic extended-response question.

terms.d: An undifferentiated cell of an organism which is capable of giving rise to many more cells of the same type, and from which certain other cells can arise from differentiation.
A cell that has not yet become specialised for a particular function.
The process by which a cell changes to become specialised for its job.
A cell with a structure adapted to carry out a particular function.
A stem cell from an early embryo that can differentiate into most types of human cell.
A stem cell found in adult tissue, e.g. bone marrow, that can form many types of cell including blood cells.
Soft tissue inside some bones where blood cells are made; contains adult stem cells.
Plant tissue at the tips of roots and shoots containing stem cells that can differentiate into any plant cell type throughout life.
Producing an embryo with the same genes as the patient so stem cells from it can be used for treatment without being rejected.
A genetically identical copy of an organism or cell.
An inherited blood disorder in which red blood cells are abnormally shaped; can be treated with a bone marrow transplant.
When the patient's immune system attacks transplanted cells or tissue because it sees them as foreign.
Cell division producing two genetically identical daughter cells; how stem cells make more cells.
Growing cells or tissue in a sterile nutrient medium, used to clone plants from meristem.
A question of right and wrong that people may disagree about, e.g. destroying embryos.
A condition where blood glucose is not controlled because the pancreas does not make enough insulin (type 1) or cells do not respond to it.

worked.ans: A stem cell is an **undifferentiated** cell that can **divide** to make more cells of the same type and can **differentiate** into specialised cells.
worked.q: Describe what is meant by a stem cell. (2 marks)
steps: Mark 2: can divide to produce more cells and differentiate into other types of cell.

worked.ans: Stem cells from the bone marrow of a healthy donor are transplanted into the patient. They divide and differentiate into normal red blood cells, replacing the abnormal ones. One risk is that a **virus** could be transferred from the donor cells to the patient and make them ill.
worked.q: Explain how stem cells from bone marrow can be used to treat sickle cell anaemia. Give one risk of this treatment. (4 marks)
steps: Healthy donor's bone marrow stem cells are transferred to the patient.
Stem cells divide and differentiate into healthy red blood cells.
These replace the faulty red blood cells, treating the disease.
Risk: a virus may be passed from the donor cells to the patient.

worked.ans: Embryonic stem cells can differentiate into most cell types so could be used to replace insulin-producing cells in diabetes and nerve cells in paralysis. If produced by therapeutic cloning they have the same genes as the patient so are not rejected. However, a virus may be transferred and treatments are not yet proven. Some people object on ethical or religious grounds because the embryo is destroyed and is a potential human life, although supporters point out the embryos are often spare IVF embryos that would be discarded. Overall, because of the potential to cure serious diseases, the benefits could outweigh the concerns if strict regulation is used, though adult stem cells avoid the ethical issue where they can be used.
worked.q: Evaluate the use of embryonic stem cells in treating diseases such as diabetes and paralysis. (6 marks)
steps: Define embryonic stem cells: from early embryos, can become most cell types.
Benefits: could replace insulin-producing cells and nerve cells; therapeutic cloning gives same genes so no rejection.
Risks: virus transfer; treatments still in development.
Ethical: embryo destroyed, potential human life, religious objections; counter: unwanted IVF embryos would be destroyed anyway.
